Culture.title: ‘She set out to buy a painting a day’: on the trail of Peggy Guggenheim’s legendary shopping spree
Culture.summary: Royal Academy, London The modernist collector once ran a gallery in London – but from this confusing exhibition, it’s hard to tell what exactly was once in there Peggy Guggenheim, art enthusiast and socialite born into a wealthy New York family, was often photographed outside her palazzo in Venice with a handbag dog and outré sunglasses. The Peggy Guggenheim Collection as we now know it, however, was nearly not in her Venice palazzo but London, evidenced by a short-lived and largely overlooked period between January 1938 and June 1939 when she ran Guggenheim Jeune in Cork Street. This exhibition posits that this initial gallery’s activities were far more influential in the shaping of contemporary art than previously recognised. Guggenheim Jeune mounted a flurry of 20 exhibitions including such UK firsts as a group show dedicated to collage, and solo exhibitions by Wassily Kandinsky , Jean Cocteau and Yves Tanguy . How to demonstrate the pioneering qualities of a gallery that is now a ghost? With reassembling and contextual padding, it appears. The catalogue states that at least 60% of the artworks in this exhibition were originally shown at Guggenheim Jeune, though only a handful of captions list definitive instances. Does this imply that where not stated, they are included for illustrative purposes? This may be due to relevant works being difficult to obtain; for the segment representing Jean Cocteau’s exhibition in January 1938 we have one of his ink drawings for his 1937 play Les Chevaliers de la Table Ronde, and another in reproduction only. Continue reading...

Culture.title: They’re one of the UK’s greatest cult bands – who swore they’d never reunite. What brought Life Without Buildings back together?
Culture.summary: The Scottish quartet existed for just three years at the turn of the millennium. But after Frank Ocean and TikTok thrilled to Sue Tompkins’ unique vocals, they’re back. They explain their fears about ‘spoiling the joy’ ‘I’m excited, I’m scared, I’m anxious – that bubbling feeling, like when you’re on a rollercoaster, at the very top, just before the big drop.” On a drizzly afternoon in July, huddled with her three bandmates in the cramped cupboard that’s the dressing room of Glasgow venue Mono, Sue Tompkins is managing her feelings ahead of her first proper gig with Life Without Buildings in almost a quarter of a century. “Everybody coming is invited, it’s secret, nobody paid much to get in, the profits are going to charity,” adds guitarist Robert Dallas Gray, sat beside her, as much to steady his own nerves as to explain the circumstances of tonight’s show. “I hope people aren’t looking at it like we’re fucking entertainers .” Continue reading...

Culture.title: ‘Mick Jagger should fold up his penis and go home’: the caustic genius of music critic Robert Christgau
Culture.summary: Beloved for his savage takedowns and rhapsodic raves, the legendary Village Voice reviewer opens up in a candid new documentary Rows and rows of CDs, albums, cassettes and books creak and groan on shelves that snake around the walls and choke the halls of an apartment in New York City’s East Village. The clutter that sprawls through its rooms is so dense it suggests the twistiest parts of a Moroccan medina or a warren no self-respecting rabbit would allow. Buried amid the muddle is a man hunched over a computer keyboard, clacking out words meant to make sense of all the sounds that this physical media holds. Welcome to the lair of Robert Christgau, the self-declared “Dean of American Rock Critics”, as seen in a new documentary provocatively titled The Last Critic . “Bob is someone who has probably listened to more music, and published more words about music, than anyone to walk the face of the earth, and he’s still doing it in his mid-80s,” says Matty Wishnow, who directed the film. “It’s a career that’s both unprecedented and unrepeatable.” Continue reading...

Culture.title: American Doctor review – medics put their lives on the line in Gaza amid the carnage
Culture.summary: Poh Si Teng’s powerful documentary follows three doctors from the US who sign up to volunteer at the Nasser hospital This is the latest documentary about medics travelling to Palestine to treat civilian casualties; it’s a powerful, angry film, in a state of despair at the scale of suffering and devastation. A sliver of hope is the trio of doctors it profiles, individuals acting on their conscience. (The same can be said of director Poh Si Teng , who quit her job at ABC News and cashed in her savings to get the documentary off the ground.) It follows three American doctors who sign up to volunteer at the Nasser hospital in southern Gaza in early 2025 – though one of the trio, Thaer Ahmad, an ER doctor of Palestinian heritage from Chicago, is refused entry the night before they enter Gaza. His colleagues, Dr Feroze Sidhwa, a trauma surgeon, and Dr Mark Perlmutter, a Jewish-American orthopaedic surgeon, complete the mission. This is not the first time in Gaza for either of them. Before he leaves, Perlmutter packs antibiotics into a dozen or so little plastic bags dotted around his luggage; that way if he gets turned back at the border, he stands a chance of getting some of the life-saving medication through. Given the high death rate of medics in the war, he also gets a will drawn up before he goes. Continue reading...
